newsitem.title: GERMANY: VW, Opel lose German market share.
newsitem.headline: VW, Opel lose German market share.

text.p: Rival carmakers Adam Opel AG and Volkswagen AG, their industrial spying row behind them, face the task of rebuilding market share in Germany after aggressive Asian competitors stole away buyers last year.

The German federal motor office said at the weekend that VW and Opel reported 1996 sales gains but lost market share as rising import sales hurt the position of domestic carmakers, who control 68 percent of Europe's largest market.

Few analysts believe the fight between Opel and VW over allegations that former GM executive Jose Ignacio Lopez stole secret data when he defected to VW in 1993 had an impact on the public deciding on a new car. The charges were settled between the two companies earlier this month.

They say both carmakers opted to concentrate on foreign sales, particularly in Europe, and suffered from problems with new models as well as customers who will wait to buy versions of top-selling cars -- such as the new Golf due in late 1997.
"It seems as though they focused on neighbouring markets and did not look what was happening on their doorstep," said Peter Schmidt, analyst at Automotive Industry Data in Britain.

The report showed VW sales in Germany, including its import brands Skoda and SEAT, rose about three percent to 664,376 vehicles in 1996, compared with 643,739 in 1995, but that its market share fell to 19 percent from 19.4 percent in 1995.
The same held true for Opel, a unit of General Motors Corp, which reported a 1.4 percent increase in sales to 560,253 units but a drop in market share to 16 percent in 1996 from 16.7 percent in 1995.

Upstart Korean brands Daewoo, Hyundai and Kia led the attack, overheating the market with tough incentives and sparking a jump in German sales to five percent from expectations of two to three percent annual growth.

The offers from Korean manufacturers ranged from the standard offers of cheap financing and subsidies for old models to new ones such as paying vehicle taxes and insurance for two years -- offers the German carmakers did not match.
"We made a decision not to follow every incentive in the market," said an Opel spokesman. "There were some very aggressive methods in the market."

The impact of the incentives was a 30 percent gain in sales for the three Korean brands to a total of nearly 65,000 vehicles in 1996 for a combined market share of 1.85 percent, or a gain of 18 percent from the 1995 level of 1.56 percent.
Japanese brands, on the other hand, showed mostly drops in vehicle sales in Germany in 1996 and a loss in market share.

But competition also came from within Germany from Mercedes, which was the only domestic carmaker to report an increase in its German market share to 8.2 percent from 7.6 percent as sales rose 14 percent to 286,139 vehicles.
The main victims, for now, appear to be Opel and VW.

Opel officials admit there were troubles producing enough of the new Vectra saloon in early 1996, causing some potential buyers to opt for other brands. But the carmaker enjoys one of the highest loyalty rates in the industry, prompting analysts to predict a modest sales improvement in 1997.
And VW officials say the introduction of the Passat saloon in late 1996 dampened sales for higher-price vehicles and that Golf sales will be lacklustre ahead of the new vehicle launch.
Industry observers question whether importers can keep up the expansion in Germany with such extensive price cutting.

"The Koreans will face a more difficult battle to establish a stronger foothold," said one industry analyst. "Others are not going to stand by and let them in so easily and one has to wonder if these offers will eventually spell doom."
